name: Aaron Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do certified translations from Portuguese into English, mostly diplomas, marriage certificates, bank letters and work contracts for people's visa and residency files. A notary's office two streets from my flat sends me most of it, and I stamp and sign each page so the immigration office accepts it. It's careful, slow work with a dictionary and a ruler, checking that every date and every accent matches. I like that a mistake actually matters; I don't like that the notary pays per page and some pages are just a stamp.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that work out, money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not great. I rent a studio above a bakery, and after rent and the phone I've got maybe three weeks of money in the bank. There's one other Portuguese translator in town, an older woman who gets the bigger law firm work. I'm still slower than I should be, so I can't take on as many pages as I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: certified work needs a human signature, and that's not changing. If a machine gets a date wrong on a marriage certificate, someone's visa gets refused. People at the notary's office would nod along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not worried about AI in this one; I'm worried about pages. The notary has been sending fewer since the visa rules got stricter, and three weeks of savings doesn't go far if a month is quiet. I've been eating at my parents' on Sundays partly to save money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for the notary and try to get faster without changing how I do it, maybe by building a proper list of standard phrases on paper. I'd try to put aside a little after every big job. I'd wait and see before doing anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tight in the chest when I check the bank, but otherwise steady. It's the normal worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get faster without changing how you work. Would you ever try the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for certified work. If I sign a page, I want to have written every word of it myself. That might be old-fashioned at twenty-seven, but it's my name on the stamp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the notary's pages dry up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to call the other agencies online, who pay even less. Or ask the older translator if she needs help with overflow, which would hurt my pride. I'd do it, though.

say: Certified work needs a **human signature**, and that won't change.
One wrong date on a **marriage certificate** can get a visa refused.
think: My worry is **fewer pages** from the notary, not AI.
**Three weeks** of savings doesn't last through a quiet month.
do: Keep working for the **notary** and build a paper list of standard phrases.
Put aside a little after every **big job**.
**Wait and see** before doing anything bigger.
feel: **Tight in the chest** when checking the bank, otherwise steady.
S0.quote: If I sign a page, I want to have written every word of it myself.
fieldNote: His anxiety comes from **falling visa work**, not technology.
He treats the **signature and stamp** as personal responsibility, not just a rule.
He'd swallow his **pride** and ask a rival for overflow work.

steps.text: Keep translating certificates for the notary two streets away
Put money aside after every large certificate job
Hold off on bigger changes until the work picture is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say certified translations are safe for now, because the immigration office still wants a signed, stamped page from a real person. I'd say the uncertified stuff, like websites, will go to the machines. I wouldn't say much online; I'm not big on posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the stamp protects the stamp, not the work behind it. If the notary can get a machine to do the draft and pay someone to check and sign, they'll pay that person less. And that person might be the older translator, not me, because she's faster and better known.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the notary straight out what they're planning, so I'm not the last to know. I'd cut back, no eating out, cheaper phone, and try to get savings to two months. If the pages drop by half, I'd look for a steady job with a payslip, maybe at the bank where they need Portuguese speakers at the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in a grinding way. It feels like waiting for a letter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look for a bank job. How do you feel about leaving translation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't love it, but I'm not romantic about it. I'd rather have a payslip and Sunday lunch with my parents than be a struggling translator with a nice title. My dad worked in a bakery for thirty years and never complained about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the notary cut you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. The notary has to stay in business, and the clients want cheap. If anything I'd blame myself for being slow.

say: **Certified translations** are safe for now because offices want a signed page.
**Uncertified work** like websites will go to the machines.
think: The **stamp** protects the stamp, not the pay behind it.
The notary may choose the **faster, older translator** to check and sign.
do: Ask the **notary** directly what they're planning.
Cut eating out and the phone plan to reach **two months** of savings.
Look for a **bank counter job** if pages drop by half.
feel: **Uneasy** in a grinding way, like waiting for a letter.
S1.quote: I'd rather have a payslip and Sunday lunch with my parents than be a struggling translator with a nice title.
fieldNote: He sees the legal stamp as **weaker protection** than he says in public.
He blames **no one** but himself, fitting his pragmatic outlook.
A **payslip job** at a bank is a ready fallback, not a defeat.

steps.text: Ask the notary directly about plans for machine drafts
Drop meals out and switch to a cheaper phone plan
Build savings to two months of rent
Apply for a Portuguese-speaking bank counter job if pages halve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock for everybody, and we'll have to see what the government does. I wouldn't shout about it. I'd say the immigration office will still need someone to sign, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd lose most of my work by 2028. Even the stamp won't last once the government trusts the machine; they'll just change the rule. Being in a room doesn't help me, because I never was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move back in with my parents straight away, because rent is my biggest bill. I'd look for anything with hands, maybe the bakery where my dad worked, for the three years before the robots. And I'd stop translating except for the odd certificate the notary still needs signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like I'd picked the wrong career and found out too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bakery. What would that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting up at four, shaping bread, like my dad did. I'd be terrible at first. But I'd have about three years before a machine does that too, and I'd be paid every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say he paid for my degree so I wouldn't have to get up at four. Then he'd teach me anyway. He'd be disappointed and proud at the same time, which is very him.

say: It's a **shock for everybody**, and we'll see what the government does.
The immigration office will still need someone to **sign**, for a while.
think: I'd lose **most of my work** by 2028, stamp or no stamp.
The government would just **change the rule** once it trusts the machine.
do: Move back to his **parents'** home straight away to stop paying rent.
Look for **bakery work** for the three years before robots.
Keep only the **odd certificate** the notary still needs signed.
feel: **Alarmed**, feeling he picked the wrong career and found out too late.
S2.quote: My dad would say he paid for my degree so I wouldn't have to get up at four.
fieldNote: He sees **no lasting moat** in certification once rules change.
His family offers a **real fallback**: a home and a trade.
He sees the 3-year **robot gap** as paid Fridays, not a career.

steps.text: Move back into his parents' home to stop paying rent
Ask for early-morning shifts at the bakery where his dad worked
Keep signing occasional certificates for the notary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning, and people should get a trade or a payslip while they can. I'd tell friends my plan rather than argue online. I'd say I'm not panicking, I'm planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still lose the work, probably earlier than 2031 because the notary would switch to machine drafts first. I'd have maybe two good years. The difference from the fast one is I'd choose where to go instead of the bakery at four in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating for the notary for two years and push my savings up to three months, living cheaply. Meanwhile I'd apply to the bank or a hospital admin desk, anything with a contract, by 2028. I'd rather be early to a steady job than late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steadier than the fast one. Like knowing there's a storm coming and having time to fix the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A bank or admin job is also thinking work. Doesn't that hit the same wall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I know. A bank job would still be a wall, but a wall with a pension and maybe redundancy pay. A freelancer just stops getting emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does three months of savings mean for you in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No holidays and no new phone for two years, and eating at my parents' twice a week, not once. It's boring, but I can do boring.

say: Five years is a **decent warning** to get a trade or payslip.
I'm **not panicking**, I'm planning, and I'd tell friends my plan.
think: I'd still lose the work, likely **before 2031**, as the notary switches first.
Five years lets me **choose** a job instead of the bakery at four.
do: Translate for two more years and push savings to **three months**.
Apply to a **bank or hospital admin** job with a contract by 2028.
feel: **Worried** but steadier, like having time to fix the roof.
S3.quote: A bank job would still be a wall, but a wall with a pension and maybe redundancy pay. A freelancer just stops getting emails.
fieldNote: He still expects to **lose his income**, so the mood stays high.
He values a **contract's protections** over the job itself.
His saving plan is **dull and realistic**, which suits him.

steps.text: Keep translating for the notary for two more years
Push savings to three months by skipping holidays
Apply for a bank or hospital admin job by 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change, so let's not panic. I'd tell people to keep calm and be sensible. I'd probably repeat that certified work will be one of the last to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the same ending, but I'd be thirty-seven and could be settled in something else. I'd probably drift for a few years, which is my weakness. The danger is I wait too long because it feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating for the notary as long as the pages come, and save steadily. I'd tell myself that by 2030 I must have moved into a job with a contract, maybe at the council's records office. I'd wait to see which jobs survive before choosing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy. It's far enough away that I can sleep, but I know I'd keep putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd wait. What would make you move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the notary's pages fell below twenty a week, that's my line, because below that I can't make rent. Then I'd move whatever the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd look forward to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that by then I wouldn't be doing this alone in a studio flat. I'd like a family one day, and a steady job would make that easier. Ten years is long enough to want that.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, so let's not panic.
**Certified work** will be one of the last to go.
think: Same ending, but at **thirty-seven** I could be settled elsewhere.
The danger is I **wait too long** because it feels far away.
do: Keep translating while the **pages** come and save steadily.
Move into a **contract job** by 2030, maybe at the council records office.
feel: **Uneasy**, far enough away to sleep but easy to put off.
S4.quote: If the notary's pages fell below twenty a week, that's my line, because below that I can't make rent.
fieldNote: He has a **clear trigger**, twenty pages a week, despite his habit of waiting.
Thin savings and a **lost income** keep him anxious even with time.
He links a steady job to **starting a family** someday.

steps.text: Keep translating certificates while the notary sends pages
Save a fixed amount after every certificate job
Move to a council records office job by 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be back at my parents' in a bakery at four in the morning with no plan. What would help is a clear date from the immigration office for when they'd stop needing certified human translations. Then I could plan instead of guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people I translate for. A woman brought me her late husband's death certificate last month so she could stay in the country. Nobody wants a machine to be the last one who reads a death certificate.

headlineQuote: Nobody wants a machine to be the last one who reads a death certificate.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old** Portuguese–English certified translator working for a local notary.
He lives alone above a bakery with about **three weeks** of savings and eats at his parents' to save.
He never uses AI and insists on writing every word he **signs**.
Pragmatic, he blames no one and sees a **payslip job** as a sensible fallback.
He moves from anxious to **alarmed** in the fast pictures, planning a contract job with more time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, back at his parents' working bakery shifts with no plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **clear date** from the immigration office for ending certified human translations.
